title: Elodie and the Gravity
premise: Odile Delacroix, a cargo hauler who survived the fall of his homeworld by erasing every trace of who he was, answers a distress beacon broadcasting in Old Meridian—a language only he and a handful of scattered refugees still know. The message it carries is a verified ceasefire order from the war's original architects, proof that both governments have been fighting on fabricated authority for two decades. Every faction wants the signal destroyed, and Odile's own hidden identity makes him the one courier who can authenticate it—and the one man whose delivery will expose him to arrest, or worse. He delivers the message at terrible cost: his ship, his anonymity, and the quiet life he built, but in exchange the war ends and the Meridian diaspora, himself included, finally has somewhere to belong.
about_author: Petra Fairweather is the pen name of a former maritime insurance adjuster who traded harbor offices for deep-space fiction after a career spent investigating disasters no one wanted to explain. She writes about people who survive by staying small, and what happens when the universe refuses to let them.

chapters.title: Dead Language, Live Signal
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Hauling scrap through the contested Verge, Odile intercepts a distress ping in Old Meridian and nearly deletes it—until he realizes he's the only person in range who can read it. The beat is dread disguised as routine; invisibility has been his religion for seven years, and something just prayed to him in his mother tongue.

chapters.title: The Wreck That Shouldn't Float
chapters.summary: Odile boards the derelict relay station Kestrel-9 and finds its last survivor, an old archivist named Maren Voss, dying with a data core clutched to her chest. She names him by his real name—the one he buried—and dies asking him to carry the message to Concord Station. The beat is grief reawakened; his past has found him and refuses to stay dead.

chapters.title: Cargo Manifest of One
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, intercut with flashbacks to the fall of Meridian. He weighs running versus delivering, auditing his own survival like a claims report: what did staying invisible actually cost him? A patrol frigate demands inspection, forcing him to hide the core in plain sight among legitimate freight. The beat is cold calculation cracking into resolve—he decides, almost despite himself, to go to Concord.

chapters.title: The Tollgate
chapters.summary: At the neutral port of Halcyon Reach, Odile seeks forged transit papers from a smuggler queen, Iyo Sarn, who recognizes the data core's encryption signature—and offers triple its weight in credits to sell it to the Coalition instead. The chapter is temptation in a warm bar; belonging, Odile realizes, can be bought, but only ever as a counterfeit.

chapters.title: What the Core Remembers
chapters.summary: Odile decrypts fragments: the ceasefire order is genuine, signed by the founders of both warring states, suppressed when their successors chose profitable war over peace. His POV alternates with a Coalition intelligence officer, Captain Reyes, who has traced the distress signal and is hunting the courier. The beat is vertigo—the truth is real, and now two governments want him erased.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Reyes corners Odile in Halcyon's docking bays, offering amnesty for the core and exposure of his fugitive identity if he refuses. Odile escapes by blowing his own cargo—his livelihood, his home—out into the dark. The beat is sacrifice made concrete: the price of survival was never money, it was everything he pretended to be.

chapters.title: The Long Fall to Concord
chapters.summary: Running dark in a borrowed skiff, Odile crosses the blockade line with Reyes in pursuit and Iyo's betrayal closing from behind. A near-fatal micrometeorite strike forces him to repair the ship while reciting Meridian funeral rites aloud, alone. The beat is stripped-bare endurance; with nothing left to hide behind, he finally admits the message matters more than his life.

chapters.title: Concord Station Falls Silent
chapters.summary: Odile slips into Concord during a station-wide lockdown and finds the diplomatic summit already hijacked—hardliners on both sides have cut communications to prevent any peace reaching the delegates. Reyes catches him at gunpoint, but hesitates when Odile plays her a fragment of the order in her own grandmother's language. The beat is the enemy becoming human; power corrupts, but it doesn't reach everyone.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Climax. Odile and Reyes fight their way to the station's primary transmitter while hardliner marines seal the chamber. Out of options, Odile authenticates the order live, speaking Old Meridian on open channels so every refugee ship in the system hears a language they thought extinct declare the war illegitimate. The beat is triumphant exposure—his name, his origin, his crime of existing, all broadcast to save everyone else.

chapters.title: Gravity, Released
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, weeks later. The ceasefire holds; tribunals begin; Iyo faces judgment and Reyes testifies on his behalf. Stripped of his ship and his alias, Odile stands in a resettlement hall where Meridian survivors are teaching children the old tongue, and someone offers him a seat. The beat is quiet arrival: belonging was never granted, it was built—and for the first time, he stays.
